title: 道德經 第三十三章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 33, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 69. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 33 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 辯德 (Telling Potency Apart). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
知人者智，
自知者明。

morph.gloss: to know, to have the measure of
the one who — 者 turns the whole clause before it into a noun
clever, knowing; cleverness — shrewd calculation, not wisdom in the good sense
oneself — the reflexive always stands BEFORE its verb
clear-sighted, discerning; the light by which a thing is seen for what it is

sentences.l:
The one who knows others — clever;
the one who knows himself — clear-sighted.
sentences.i: To know others is cleverness; to know yourself is clear sight.
sentences.n: The chapter is eight maxims of one build, and 者 makes every one of them: put after a clause it turns the whole of it into a noun, 'the one who ——'. There is no verb 'to be' in any of them; the English 'is' is ours each time. The pair here turns on two words for knowing that are not the same thing at all. 智 is cleverness — calculating, aimed outward, at other people; 明 is the light a thing is seen by, and in this book it is nearly always turned inward. Wang Bi says it flatly: knowing others is cleverness and no more, and does not come up to knowing oneself, which passes above cleverness altogether. Note also 自: the reflexive stands before its verb, so 自知 is 'know oneself', never 'oneself knows'.

sentences.t:
勝人者有力，
自勝者強。

morph.gloss: to overcome, to get the better of
force, muscle — strength in the arm, the strength that throws a man down
strong (qiáng, the stative reading; qiǎng would be 'to force')

sentences.l:
The one who gets the better of others has muscle;
the one who gets the better of himself is strong.
sentences.n: 力 and 強 are not two words for the same quality. 力 is force in the arm, what it takes to put another man down; 強 is strength as holding, lasting, not being moved. Wang Bi turns the whole chapter on one hinge here: to spend your cleverness on other men is not as good as spending it on yourself, and to spend your force on other men is not as good as spending it on yourself — for the light used on oneself leaves nothing in you for things to dodge behind, and force used on oneself leaves nothing in you for things to alter. Watch 強: two maxims further on the same character is read qiǎng and means something else.

morph.gloss: enough, sufficient (the character is also 'the foot')

sentences.l: The one who knows enough — rich.
sentences.i: To know when you have enough is wealth.
sentences.n: Four characters, and the maxim at its barest: a noun-clause, a predicate, and nothing between them. Wang Bi's comment is nearly as short — he who knows sufficiency loses nothing of himself, and so is rich. Riches, on that reading, are not what a man has but what he has stopped reaching for.

morph.gloss: to force oneself, to press on hard (qiǎng here — NOT qiáng 'strong', two lines above)
to walk, to go; to put into practice, to keep at (xíng; read háng it is 'a row, a rank')
the will, the purpose the mind is set on

sentences.l: The one who forces himself to keep at it has a will.
sentences.i: One who drives himself on has a will in him.
sentences.n: Here 強 is read qiǎng, not qiáng: not 'strong' but 'to force, to press' — 強行 is making oneself keep at the practice. Nothing in the writing tells you which reading you have; only the sense of the line does, which is why every occurrence in this text carries its reading under the character. The line is meant well, and Wang Bi says why: the man who can keep diligently at it will certainly get what he set his will on.

morph.gloss: a place, one's own station — here the plain NOUN, not the particle met before verbs
long-lasting, enduring (of time, not of length)

sentences.l: The one who does not lose his place lasts long.
sentences.n: 所 is the small word usually met standing before a verb and making a noun of it — 所惡 'what is loathed', 所以 'that whereby', both of which you have had. Here it is the plain noun it started life as: a place, the station that is one's own. Wang Bi reads the line with the two before it — see by your own light, take the measure of your own force, act within it, and you do not lose your place.

morph.gloss: to perish, to be lost, to be gone for good
long life, length of days; the full span

sentences.l: The one who dies and yet does not perish has length of days.
sentences.i: To die and not be lost — that is length of days.
sentences.n: The line is disputed, and honestly so. Early texts write 亡 'to perish' and 忘 'to forget' for each other, and taken the second way this says 'dies and is not forgotten' — a fine sentiment, and probably not this one. Wang Bi takes 亡 straight: though the body goes under, the way of life that was in it does not perish, and so the man gets the whole of his span. We follow him and record the other. One more thing, about the sound. The chapter's rhyme is a run, not a pair: 富, 志 and 久 all belong to the 之 rhyme group, and 壽 comes from the neighbouring 幽 group, a crossing this book makes freely. Mandarin has kept only a fragment of it — 久 jiǔ and 壽 shòu still chime, 富 fù and 志 zhì have drifted out — so what you can hear at the end is Mandarin's own accident rather than the old rhyme surviving whole.
